paras: The warning to Black residents of Bloomfield, Indiana, was a letter received in mid-July 1903 by Charles Shelton, a Black resident of the Greene County town, ordering all Black people to leave the county by July 25. The letter claimed to come from a "committee" of citizens of nearby Linton and threatened that those who stayed would "receive a visit." Papers treated it as an outgrowth of anti-Black feeling at Linton, where a mob had just driven out a group of Black waiters.

Linton was a Greene County mining town that, according to an Indianapolis Journal dispatch, had not allowed Black people to live there since Black miners brought from Kentucky by a coal company were driven away years earlier. In early July 1903, Terre Haute caterer Alec Sandison brought Black waiters to Linton for an Elks' banquet and was ordered to send them out of town, which he did as a crowd the Journal put at two thousand hastened their departure. Eugene Debs called on the United Mine Workers to discipline its Linton members for their part in that demonstration.

A Bloomfield special dated July 17 reported that a letter from Linton, written by a "committee" purporting to be made up of Linton citizens, had reached Charles Shelton, whom the Louisville Courier-Journal called "an inoffensive colored resident." The letter stated that if all the Black residents of the town did not leave Greene County by July 25 they would "receive a visit" from the committee. A later Bloomfield item, dated July 20, described Shelton as "a leading colored man" and gave the threat as being "waited upon" if they did not go before the 25th.

Both reports described alarm among Bloomfield's Black residents, the Jasper paper noting that the women especially were "much alarmed." No report of departures, of any visit by the committee, or of an effort to identify the letter's writers appears in the coverage.

The Courier-Journal carried the story on its front page on July 18 under the headline "WARNED TO LEAVE. Consternation Prevails Among Negroes of Bloomfield," describing Linton as a town "where the hatred against the negro is very bitter." The Jasper Weekly Courier ran a brief "Warned to Leave" item on July 24 that attributed the fear to "the enmity against their race at Linton." Both accounts were sympathetic in tone toward Bloomfield's Black residents and tied the letter to the Linton riot, while neither named a suspect.
No Black-press coverage of the Bloomfield letter was found.

bases: A written notice from a self-styled Linton 'committee' ordered the Black residents of Bloomfield to leave Greene County by July 25 under threat of a 'visit' (A2, A3); no departures or violence after the deadline appear in the coverage.

Two white Indiana-area reports with different datelines (July 17 and July 20) and different wording agree that Charles Shelton received the Linton 'committee' letter ordering Black residents out by the 25th (A2, A3).
